cases.is: A unified indirect tax replaced a patchwork of state and central levies to create a single national market.
High central excise on fuel funds the budget but feeds cost-push pressure across the economy.

cases.t: Onion price volatility and export bans
cases.is: Sharp onion price spikes after monsoon shocks triggered export bans to protect consumers.

cases.t: Minimum Support Prices for wheat and rice
cases.is: Minimum support prices, backed by government procurement mainly of wheat and rice, act as a price floor for farmers who can sell to the state; fear that three 2020 farm laws would weaken this system, and a demand for a legal MSP guarantee, were central to the 2020-21 farmer protests.
Free or heavily subsidised power encourages over-pumping of groundwater and fiscal strain.

cases.t: Sin taxes on tobacco and alcohol
cases.is: High taxes on demerit goods aim to cut consumption and raise revenue.
China's control of rare-earth processing gives it market power and a strategic lever in trade.
Large production and consumption subsidies helped build a dominant EV industry, alongside scale, competition and battery learning.
A state monopoly is the world's largest cigarette producer by volume, mixing revenue and a major demerit good.

cases.t: Beijing air pollution and industrial emissions
cases.is: Heavy-industry emissions imposed severe health costs, prompting pollution caps.
Loans, quotas and import limits keep domestic sugar prices above world levels.
City taxes on sweetened drinks (Berkeley 2015, Philadelphia 2017) aim to cut consumption and fund services.
A market for emissions permits prices carbon to cut greenhouse gases efficiently; in 2025 the programme was extended to 2045 and renamed cap-and-invest.
Aggressive marketing and addiction created vast external and information costs.
A phased rise to a $15 hourly minimum under Seattle's 2014 ordinance tested employment vs income effects of a wage floor.
Dominance in ticketing and venues raised antitrust concerns over prices and fees.
Subsidies and historic price supports shape EU farming and trade.
Abolishing production quotas exposed the sugar market to freer competition.
‘Roam like at home' regulation removed cross-border mobile surcharges.
Bans on selected items, consumption-reduction targets and producer-responsibility charges target plastic pollution as a negative externality.
Guaranteed feed-in prices, paid for by a levy on electricity bills, helped drive a rapid expansion of renewable generation.
A tiered levy on sugary drinks pushed reformulation rather than just price rises.
A small per-bag charge sharply cut single-use bag use.
A daily charge prices road use to cut congestion, an external cost.
A floor price per unit targets cheap, high-strength alcohol (50p per unit from 2018, 65p from 2024).
Default enrolment dramatically raised workplace pension participation.
A deemed-consent default aimed to raise consent to organ donation.
Tax exemptions and perks helped make Norway the country with the highest electric share of new-car sales.
An auctioned quota of vehicle entitlements caps car ownership to manage congestion and scarcity.
Tiered water pricing reflects scarcity and funds supply security.
Cutting costly fuel subsidies freed funds but raised prices and protests.

Removing the petrol subsidy in May 2023 sharply raised pump and transport costs and cut a large fiscal cost, but by end-2023 pump prices were again capped below cost, so an implicit subsidy returned; check the current position before citing it.
Coordinated output cuts by a cartel support oil prices.
Standardised packaging reduced the appeal of a demerit good.
Emissions fell while the economy grew after Sweden introduced an early, high carbon tax in 1991; studies credit the tax with part of the fall, notably in transport, rather than all of it.
Free vaccination at government centres aimed to internalise a positive consumption externality at scale.

cases.t: Right to Education and schooling subsidies
cases.is: Free, compulsory schooling for ages 6–14 treats education as a merit good with wide benefits.
A nationwide ban on specified single-use plastics targets pollution.
Dynamic pricing clears demand spikes but raises fairness concerns.

cases.t: App-store fees and the Digital Markets Act
cases.is: New rules target ‘gatekeeper' platform power over app distribution and fees.
Fines that set EU antitrust records at the time (Shopping 2017, Android 2018) targeted abuse of search and Android dominance.
Ultra-low pricing reshaped an oligopoly and forced consolidation.
Booming US demand and supply shocks drove avocado price swings.
Low elasticities and weather shocks make coffee prices highly volatile.
For status-driven luxuries, quantity demanded can rise with price (Veblen effect).

A rent ceiling froze, and in some cases cut, Berlin rents until Germany's Federal Constitutional Court declared it void in 2021 because rent law is a federal matter; its effect on the supply of flats to rent is a separate, evidential question.

From 2023 the Inflation Reduction Act capped what US Medicare enrollees pay out of pocket for insulin at $35 a month; the cap limits the patient's share of the cost, not the price at which insulin is sold.
Cheap clothing production carries environmental and labour external costs.
Severe drought pushed a major city near to running out of water.
Historic supply control by a dominant firm sustained high diamond prices.
Open-access fisheries are over-exploited beyond sustainable yields.
Public immunisation programmes generate large positive external benefits.
Off-grid solar and micro-grids extend power where networks under-supply.
An EU-wide cap-and-trade market, also covering Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, prices carbon for power, heavy industry, aviation and (since 2024) shipping.
Overnight withdrawal of high-value notes aimed at black money disrupted cash-based activity.
A large relief and credit package supported the economy through the pandemic shock.
A statutory CPI inflation target of 4% (±2%), set for five-year periods, aimed to anchor monetary policy and expectations.
Strong GDP growth coexisted with weak formal job creation; official unemployment fell, so the debate is over job quality.
Output-linked subsidies aim to build manufacturing capacity and exports.
Large subsidies and capex pressure the deficit and debt path.
Massive investment-led stimulus countered the global financial crisis.
A property-developer debt crisis threatened growth and confidence; Evergrande was ordered into liquidation in January 2024.
Weak domestic demand and industrial overcapacity pushed prices toward deflation, risking a debt-deflation spiral.
Growth slowed as the easy gains from catch-up faded.
A large package combined green subsidies, tax measures and deficit goals; many of its clean-energy tax credits were curtailed by 2025 legislation.
Rapid rate rises aimed to bring down post-pandemic inflation.
A housing and banking collapse caused a deep global recession.
Large-scale asset purchases eased policy when rates hit zero.
Cheques, expanded benefits and loans cushioned the pandemic shock.
Inflation jumped on demand recovery, supply bottlenecks and energy.
A collapse in demand, deepened by bank failures and monetary contraction, caused mass unemployment and shaped Keynesian thought.
Corporate and income tax cuts aimed to lift investment and growth.
High debt and lost competitiveness within the euro forced bailouts and austerity.
Asset purchases and negative rates fought low inflation across the eurozone.
A joint borrowing-funded recovery package marked a fiscal step-change.
Unfunded tax cuts spooked bond markets; the gilt sell-off, amplified by pension funds' liability-driven investment strategies, forced Bank of England intervention and a reversal.
Operational independence aimed to make monetary policy credible.
Wage subsidies preserved jobs through lockdowns.
‘Three arrows' of monetary easing, fiscal spending and reform fought deflation.
Stagnation and near-zero rates illustrated the limits of monetary policy.
Money printing to cover deficits, amid collapsing output, caused extreme hyperinflation.
Collapsing output and money printing produced hyperinflation.
Cutting rates into high inflation worsened price instability and the lira; policy reversed to sharp rate rises from June 2023.
Sharp fiscal austerity aimed to crush triple-digit inflation.

cases.t: Inflation targeting and the Real Plan
cases.is: A new currency and later inflation targeting tamed chronic inflation.
Post-crisis recession drove very high youth and structural unemployment.
A reform plan aims to reduce oil dependence and broaden the economy.
Saving oil revenue smooths spending and shares wealth across generations.
State-directed industrial policy is widely credited, though debated, with building export champions and growth.
The first explicit inflation target became a global model.
Debt, reserve loss and policy errors caused default and shortages.
Repeated borrowing-limit fights risked default and confidence.
A gas-price shock drove a severe cost-push inflation episode.

cases.t: Youth unemployment: a series high and a change of method
cases.is: High graduate unemployment exposed labour-market mismatch; the official 16–24 series was suspended after its 2023 high and resumed in 2024 on a method that excludes students, so the two are not comparable.
Shipping and component shortages raised costs across sectors.
Oil-price shocks produced simultaneous inflation and unemployment.
Unemployment benefits and progressive taxes cushioned the downturn automatically.

cases.t: Negative interest rates in the euro area
cases.is: Sub-zero policy rates (2014–22) aimed to push lending and spending.
A shrinking workforce constrains long-run growth potential.
Deficits financed by money creation, worsened by reparations and the 1923 Ruhr occupation, produced classic hyperinflation.
High savings, education and openness drove rapid sustained growth.

cases.t: Switzerland deflation and a strong franc
cases.is: Safe-haven currency strength imported deflationary pressure.
Heavy public capex raises growth but can crowd out private borrowing.
High inflation and wage demands raised fears of a self-feeding spiral.

cases.t: Stability and Growth Pact fiscal rules
cases.is: Common deficit and debt limits constrain national fiscal policy across the EU, most tightly in the eurozone; suspended in 2020–23, the rules were reformed in 2024 around country-specific expenditure paths.
Tit-for-tat tariffs from 2018 targeted the bilateral deficit and technology rivalry.
‘National security' tariffs raised input costs for downstream industries; the rates were raised in 2025.

cases.t: Brexit and leaving the single market
cases.is: Exiting the EU customs union and single market raised trade frictions.

cases.t: The EU single market (1993) and customs union (1968)
cases.is: Free movement of goods, services, capital and labour deepened integration.
A deal with zero tariffs and quotas on goods that meet rules of origin, but not frictionless, governs post-Brexit trade.
A renegotiated North American agreement updated rules of origin and labour.

cases.t: RCEP: the largest free-trade agreement by members' combined GDP
cases.is: A 15-economy Asia-Pacific agreement lowered tariffs and harmonised rules.
A high-standard trans-Pacific FTA continued after US withdrawal and admitted the UK in 2024.
A continental FTA aims to boost intra-African trade and industrialisation.
Multilateral trade talks stalled over agriculture and development issues.
Joining the WTO accelerated export-led growth and global integration.
Large overseas infrastructure lending deepened global economic ties.
A managed-float currency was labelled a ‘manipulator' by the US Treasury in August 2019, a label dropped in January 2020, although the IMF then judged the renminbi broadly in line with fundamentals.
A weaker rupee raised the cost of large oil imports and the current account deficit.
India left negotiations fearing import surges, especially from China.
Dominant reserve-currency status confers borrowing and trade advantages.
A large goods deficit is usually explained by saving-investment and currency factors.
A single currency removed exchange-rate risk among members.
Inside the euro, Greece could not devalue to restore competitiveness.
Abandoning a currency floor caused a sudden franc surge.
Restrictions on advanced chips and tools target strategic technology.
A sharp yen slide prompted currency intervention and policy debate.
Currency instability led to controls and parallel exchange rates; most controls on individuals were lifted in April 2025.
Repeated devaluations and an IMF programme addressed external imbalance.
Letting the naira float aimed to end distortions from a managed rate.
Coordinated intervention aimed to weaken an over-strong dollar, which had been falling since its February 1985 peak and fell much further after the accord.
Pegged currencies and capital flight triggered a regional crisis from Thailand.
Sweeping sanctions cut trade and finance after the invasion of Ukraine.
War-driven energy and food shocks rippled through the world economy.
Heavy reliance on imported gas became a strategic vulnerability.

cases.t: OPEC+ and the terms of trade
cases.is: Output decisions shift oil prices and exporters' terms of trade.
Tariffs and bans on Australian exports followed a diplomatic dispute; China lifted most of them in 2023–24.
A long WTO fight concerned government subsidies to aircraft makers; the retaliatory tariffs were suspended in 2021 (check their current status).

A carbon border charge, paid by importers through certificates priced on the EU carbon market, aims to prevent ‘carbon leakage'; 2023–25 was a reporting-only phase and financial obligations apply to imports from 2026, with certificates bought from 2027.
Tariffs on subsidised Chinese EVs aimed to protect domestic industry.
Low-cost garment exports drove integration and development.
Firms diversified production toward Vietnam and others to cut China reliance.
Proximity to the US drew investment as firms shortened supply chains.
A resource boom can crowd out manufacturing via currency appreciation.

cases.t: Commodity dependence and terms of trade
cases.is: Reliance on a few commodities exposes income to price swings.

cases.t: Remittances and the balance of payments
cases.is: On World Bank estimates India was the world's largest remittance recipient in 2023, and these inflows support the external accounts.
Small economies reliant on tourism were hit hard by the pandemic shock.
Anti-dumping and anti-subsidy duties on Chinese panels aimed to protect domestic makers.
A long dispute over banana import preferences pitted the EU against Latin American exporters and the US.
Signals of US tightening triggered capital outflows from emerging markets.
A regional community deepened trade and investment links in Southeast Asia.
A South American customs union shapes regional trade and external deals.
A US Treasury ‘manipulator' label (August 2019, withdrawn January 2020) escalated currency and trade tensions.
Import competition raised aggregate gains but concentrated local job losses.
Temporary protection aims to let new industries reach competitiveness.

cases.t: Bretton Woods and the dollar standard
cases.is: A post-war system of adjustable pegs to the gold-convertible dollar broke down in 1971–73: gold convertibility was suspended in 1971 and general floating followed in 1973.
Hundreds of millions of people in India exited multidimensional poverty between 2005/06 and 2019/21, on the UNDP and OPHI global MPI.
A digital ID enabled direct benefit transfers; rigorous studies find leakage fell in some programmes, while biometric checks also excluded some genuine claimants.
A rural job-guarantee scheme, legislated in 2005, provided a wage floor and safety net until the VB-G RAM G Act replaced it from 1 July 2026.
Rapid microcredit growth led to over-indebtedness and a sector crisis.
High-yield seeds and inputs transformed food output and security.
An export services boom drove growth and a skilled middle class.
Around 800 million people moved above the World Bank's international extreme-poverty line (then $1.90 a day at 2011 PPP) in the four decades to 2020, on that line and no other.
An export-oriented SEZ pioneered market reforms and FDI-led growth.
Massive infrastructure investment supported rapid development.
Surplus rural labour shifting to industry powered structural change.
Garment exports and large NGOs are widely credited with broad-based development gains.
Group-lending microcredit pioneered finance for the poor.
Mobile money brought financial services to the unbanked.
Governance reform and services investment delivered rapid gains from a low base.
Sound institutions are widely credited with turning diamond wealth into development and avoiding the resource curse.

cases.t: Oil dependence and the resource curse
cases.is: Oil reliance, volatility and weak governance constrained development.
Demand for battery minerals raised export earnings and governance risks.
State-built industrial parks attracted manufacturing FDI.
Market-oriented reforms opened the economy and accelerated growth.
Investment in education and industry is credited with taking a poor economy to high income.
Cash transfers conditional on schooling and health cut poverty.
A rigorously evaluated CCT became a global model; it was abolished in 2019.
Copper reliance and a privatised pension system shaped development debates; a 2025 reform added employer contributions to the individual-account system.
Reliance on cocoa exports exposes the economy to price swings.
Coordinated relief reduced unsustainable debt for poor countries.
A global campaign helped secure large debt write-offs (enhanced HIPC, MDRI) for poor nations.
Debt distress forced default and an IMF-supported adjustment.
An early pandemic-era default highlighted rising external-debt risks.
Repeated IMF programmes addressed recurring external crises.
Whether aid reliably promotes development remains contested.

cases.t: MDGs to the Sustainable Development Goals
cases.is: Global goals shifted from poverty targets to a broader sustainability agenda.
A randomised study in Kenya reported that school-based deworming raised school attendance, a result later disputed in re-analyses and systematic reviews.
Field experiments reshaped how poverty interventions are designed.
CCTs tie support to schooling and health to build human capital.
Migrant remittances are a major, stable source of development finance.
Girls' education yields wide social and economic returns.
Rigorous studies found microcredit's poverty impact is modest.
Tourism brings foreign exchange and jobs but heightens vulnerability.
Zones use incentives and infrastructure to attract export industry.
Whether trade access or aid better promotes development is contested.
Climate vulnerability threatens hard-won development gains.
A young, growing workforce can boost growth if jobs and skills follow.
Large-scale health funding targets diseases of poverty.
Low income, saving and investment can lock countries in a poverty cycle.
A large informal sector limits productivity, revenue and protection.
FDI brings capital, technology and jobs but can have mixed effects.

High human-development outcomes were achieved in the 1970s and 1980s, when Kerala's income per head was modest. To compare its income per head with India's, read the per capita net state domestic product table in the most recent edition of the RBI's Handbook of Statistics on Indian States.
